explanations.answer: Not one of us will give his daughter to a Benjamite
explanations.explanation: That's the oath: “Not one of us will give his daughter in marriage to a Benjamite.” The men of Israel swore it at Mizpah, and I think they had no idea how much trouble one sentence could cause. Say a thing out loud and mean it, and you can't stuff it back in the bowl. Hold onto that oath, baker, because everything else in this passage bends around it.

explanations.answer: Not one of us will set foot on Benjamite land
explanations.explanation: Close, since it's an oath about Benjamin, but that's not the one. Nothing in this passage says Israel swore off Benjamite land. What they swore was about marriage: “Not one of us will give his daughter in marriage to a Benjamite.” It's a very specific promise, and that's exactly why it becomes a problem.

explanations.answer: Not one of us will ever trade with a Benjamite
explanations.explanation: Trading never comes up in this passage, friend. The oath was about daughters: “Not one of us will give his daughter in marriage to a Benjamite.” I'd bet a whole batch that nobody wrote a trade ban into it. That one sentence is what they spend the rest of the chapter working around.

explanations.answer: Why one tribe is missing from Israel
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. They cry out, “Why, O LORD God of Israel, has this happened in Israel? Today in Israel one tribe is missing!” Notice they take the question straight to God, and they do it weeping. The tribe that's missing is Benjamin, and the people feel the hole it leaves.

explanations.answer: Why the battle took three whole days
explanations.explanation: Nothing about how long the battle lasted shows up in their cry. They're not counting days, baker. They're looking at the empty spot in Israel and asking, “Why, O LORD God of Israel, has this happened in Israel?” The ache is about a tribe, not a calendar.

explanations.answer: Why Benjamin refused to hand anyone over
explanations.explanation: That's not the question they bring to God here. Their words are about loss: “Today in Israel one tribe is missing!” They don't point a finger in this cry, they just weep. Sometimes a hurt is so big the only thing left is to ask why.

Yes, death. The oath said that “anyone who failed to come up before the LORD at Mizpah would surely be put to death.” That's a heavy promise to make, and it matters because the people are about to check who didn't show. A solemn oath is no small thing in Israel.

Exile isn't in the text, friend. The oath at Mizpah was much more serious than being sent away: anyone who didn't come up “would surely be put to death.” I know it's a heavy line. It's the reason the people start asking who was missing.
If only it were a fine, baker. You can pay a fine and go home. The text says that anyone who didn't come up before the LORD at Mizpah “would surely be put to death.” That's how serious the oath was.

Wives it is. They ask, “What should we do about wives for the survivors, since we have sworn by the LORD not to give them our daughters in marriage?” See the knot? They grieve for Benjamin and want the survivors to have wives, but their own oath is standing in the doorway. It's like being locked out with the keys sitting on the kitchen counter.

Land isn't what's worrying them here. The question on the table is about “wives for the survivors.” The oath they swore by the LORD blocks them from giving their daughters in marriage. That's the whole tangle, baker.

Leaders aren't the problem they name. They ask what to do about “wives for the survivors, since we have sworn by the LORD not to give them our daughters in marriage.” The worry is about the men who survived and the families they could have. A tribe needs families to keep going.

Jabesh-gilead is the one. The text says, “no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the camp for the assembly,” and that when the people were counted, none of its residents were there. A head count is the kind of thing nobody can talk their way around. What comes next is heavy, so I'll just say that plainly.

That name never comes up in this passage. The count turns up one town with nobody there, and it's Jabesh-gilead. The text says none of its residents were counted at the assembly. Abel-meholah is a mix-up, friend, but a fair one with names this long.

That's a mouthful, but it's not in this passage. The people count heads and find that “none of the residents of Jabesh-gilead were there.” That's the town they land on. Keep Jabesh-gilead in your pocket, baker, because it matters in the next verses.

Four hundred is right. The men found “four hundred young women who had not had relations with a man” and brought them to the camp at Shiloh in the land of Canaan. It's a sober part of the story, and I think it deserves a quiet moment. Keep that number handy, because it turns out not to be enough.

Six hundred is a real number in this story, but it belongs to someone else. It's how many Benjamite men escaped to the rock of Rimmon (Judges 20:47). The women brought from Jabesh-gilead number four hundred. That gap between the two numbers is where the trouble starts.

That's lower than what the text says, friend. The men found “four hundred young women who had not had relations with a man.” It's a heavy part of the story, so I won't joke here. Four hundred still isn't enough for everyone, as the next verse says.

The text says otherwise, baker. The Benjamites return and are given the women spared from Jabesh-gilead, but the verse adds, “But there were not enough women for all of them.” So the problem isn't solved yet. Some men are still left without wives.

False is right. The Benjamites were given the women spared from Jabesh-gilead, “But there were not enough women for all of them.” Four hundred women, and some men still without. That's why the elders have to come up with something else.

Heirs, yes. The elders say, “There must be heirs for the survivors of Benjamin, so that a tribe of Israel will not be wiped out.” A tribe only lasts if there's a next generation to carry it. That's what they're trying to protect.

Allies don't come up here. The elders want “heirs for the survivors of Benjamin, so that a tribe of Israel will not be wiped out.” A tribe survives through the families that come after, baker. That's their worry, and they say so plainly.

No weapons in this plea, friend. The elders say, “There must be heirs for the survivors of Benjamin, so that a tribe of Israel will not be wiped out.” It's a plan for the future of a tribe. They're counting on children, not swords.

explanations.answer: A feast to the LORD in Shiloh
explanations.explanation: That's it. The elders say, “there is a yearly feast to the LORD in Shiloh.” They give the spot such careful directions that you could find it with your eyes closed. A yearly feast means everyone knows when and where to look.

explanations.answer: A meeting of the elders of Israel
explanations.explanation: The elders are the ones talking, but that's not what happens at Shiloh. What they point to is “a yearly feast to the LORD in Shiloh.” So the place is already full of people, and it happens every year. Nothing here says the elders hold a meeting there.

explanations.answer: A market for traders from every tribe
explanations.explanation: No stalls or traders in this text, baker. The elders say, “there is a yearly feast to the LORD in Shiloh.” It's a feast, and it's to the LORD. I'd have loved a market with a free sample table, but that's not in the verse.

The vineyards, yes. The elders tell the Benjamites, “Go, hide in the vineyards and watch.” Rows of vines make a decent hiding place, and the Benjamites are told to wait there until the moment comes. It's a plan with a lot of waiting in it.
Olive groves are a nice guess, but they're not in the text. The elders say, “Go, hide in the vineyards and watch.” The plan is built around the vineyards, friend. No olive trees are mentioned.
Barley isn't in this plan, baker. The command is, “Go, hide in the vineyards and watch.” That's the hiding spot the elders pick for the Benjamites. Nobody is told to crouch in the grain.

explanations.answer: The daughters of Shiloh coming out to dance
explanations.explanation: That's the signal. The Benjamites are told, “When you see the daughters of Shiloh come out to perform their dances,” they are to come out of the vineyards. So the whole plan hangs on watching and waiting for that one moment. A hiding place is only as good as your patience.

explanations.answer: The priests of Shiloh coming out to pray
explanations.explanation: No priests in this plan, friend. The Benjamites are to watch for “the daughters of Shiloh” to “come out to perform their dances.” That's the cue they're given. Praying priests aren't mentioned anywhere in these verses.

explanations.answer: The fathers of Shiloh heading out to the road
explanations.explanation: The fathers do show up later, but not as the signal. The elders say the fathers or brothers will come to them “to complain,” and that's after the Benjamites have already acted. What the Benjamites watch for is “the daughters of Shiloh” coming “out to perform their dances.” Order matters in a plan like this, baker.

That's not what the elders say. Each man is to “catch for himself a wife from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.” So the plan ends with him heading home, not settling at Shiloh. Reading the whole verse saves you from a lot of wrong turns, baker.

False is right. The elders tell each man to “catch for himself a wife from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.” Nobody is told to stay and settle at Shiloh. The plan points them straight back home.

Give is the word. The elders say, “Since you did not actually give them your daughters, you have no guilt.” Their reasoning leans on that one word, because the oath was about giving a daughter. It's a lot of weight to put on a single verb, friend.

Selling isn't in their wording, baker. The elders say, “Since you did not actually give them your daughters, you have no guilt.” The oath was about giving, so giving is the word they use. A small word is carrying their whole argument.

Bringing is not what the elders say. Their words are, “Since you did not actually give them your daughters, you have no guilt.” The oath they swore was about giving a daughter, so that's the word they use. One word, and the whole speech is built on it.

True. The Benjamites did as instructed, and the text says they “went back to their own inheritance, rebuilt their cities, and settled in them.” Israel had burned the cities in Benjamin's path (Judges 20:48), so there was real rebuilding to do. I'm glad to see the tribe back on its feet, and I bet a few new kitchens went up too.

The text says they did. The Benjamites “went back to their own inheritance, rebuilt their cities, and settled in them.” The cities had been burned during the war (Judges 20:48), so rebuilding was real work. The tribe had a place to live again, baker.

explanations.answer: Back to his own tribe and inheritance
explanations.explanation: Home they go. The text says, “each of the Israelites returned from there to his own tribe and clan, each to his own inheritance.” After all that weeping, fighting and plotting, everyone heads back to their own place. Nothing says they stay.

explanations.answer: Up to Shiloh for the yearly feast
explanations.explanation: Shiloh is where the feast was, and that's where the Benjamites caught their wives. After that, the text says “each of the Israelites returned from there to his own tribe and clan, each to his own inheritance.” So nobody is sent up to Shiloh. Everybody goes home, friend.

explanations.answer: Down to Mizpah for another assembly
explanations.explanation: Mizpah was where the oath was sworn, and the text doesn't send anybody back there. It says “each of the Israelites returned from there to his own tribe and clan, each to his own inheritance.” No more assemblies this time, baker. They just go home.
